To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mechanism of long-range proton transfer in a protein depends on the position and pKa of a single amino-acid residue, which is able to shift its pKa in response to changes in charge on the redox centre.

(i) the proton-transferring module is the first long-range electron-couple proton transfer in which the mechanism has been defined at the atomic level; (ii) the proton is delivered by a rapid penetrative excursion of the side-chain of the carboxylate group of Asp 15, whose pKa is sensitive to the charge on the Fe-S cluster; and (iii) the mechanism is consistent with the requirement for a single long-lived proton-carrying group, as predicted for
the proton transfer is exquistively sensitive to the position, pK and dynamics of a single amino-acid residue, Asp15.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental mechanisms of biological electron transfer and the role of proton transfer in these processes.
the fundamental question of how energy can be stored and released in biological systems.
understanding how the chemical and physical properties of proteins are used to control biological processes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is the first time that the mechanism for long-range electron-couple proton transfer in a protein has been elucidated at atomic resolution.
the mechanism of long-range electron-couple proton transfer is defined at atomic resolution.

the proton-transferring module of ferredoxin I has an ‘active’ conformation, in which the carboxylate side chain of Asp 15 is in a position to transfer a proton to the buried Fe–S centre, and an ‘inactive’ conformation in which Asp 15 is too distant to do so.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have defined the atomic basis of the long-range proton transfer that is essential for the function of the protein ferredoxin.
we have determined, at atomic resolution and in a single long-range step, how a protein draws a proton into its core, where it is transferred to an electron-transfer active site.

we have shown that a buried iron– sulphur cluster in a protein can draw in a single solvent proton during electron transfer, and that this is a consequence of a single residue, Asp 15, which acts as an electrostatic gate for the proton.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proton is transferred through the protein matrix in a single step by the rapid penetration of the side chain carboxylate.
a single amino acid residue is sufficient to deliver a proton from the surface to the buried redox centre.
the proton transfer is exquistively sensitive to the pK of the proton donor.
